newsitem.title: USA: Clark decision sparks Chicago sell-off.
newsitem.headline: Clark decision sparks Chicago sell-off.

text.p: A court decision allowing Clark Refining and Marketing Co to restart idled units at a key Chicago-area refinery sparked a sell-off on unleaded gasoline in the local spot market on Friday, traders said.

Unleaded differentials, propped up by refiner and speculative buying since an October 19 explosion at Clark's 80,515 barrel per day Blue Island, Ill., refinery, were expected to ease once buyers could be found, traders said.
"There are all sellers out there," one Chicago trader said. "They're just looking for a bid."

An Illinois judge on Friday rejected a request by state regulators to idle the refinery until Clark could improve safety at the plant following three headline-grabbing accidents in the past two years.

The ruling cleared the way for Clark, which was running at a trimmed 55,000 barrels per day since the explosion, to double gasoline production to 2 million barrels per day when two idled units return to service, the company said.
In the Chicago spot market, prompt unleaded gasoline differentials had firmed since the explosion, opening the day at bids 8.75 cents a gallon over NYMEX December unleaded.

Clark is a key refiner in the region, producing gasoline at the Blue Island refinery and two Gulf Coast refineries that supply its 830 Midwest retail outlets and selling gasoline into the spot market.

The Illinois Attorney General had sought to idle the Blue Island refinery, which a state attorney called a "timebomb" following the October explosion, a March 1995 explosion that killed two workers and a discharge later that year that sickened more than two dozen students at a nearby high school.
The October fire was confined to a propane scrubber of an alkylation unit and damaged electrical systems, but the refinery continued operating at reduced crude rates.
Clark posted an $11.4 million loss in the third quarter on weak refining margins squeezed by high crude oil prices and weaker than expected gasoline demand.

Clark Refining is the principle operating subsidiary of St. Louis-based Clark USA, which is 46 percent owned by Toronto-based Horsham Corp, which received approval last week to merge with Trizec Corp Ltd to form Trizec Hahn Corp
